COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Main design:  Instrumental-Variables (IV) / Two-Stage Least Squares with mother fixed effects, where the random sex composition of the first two births is used as an instrument for (i) completed family size and (ii) whether a later–born child was conceived only because the parents still lacked an eldest son.  

Why IV is appropriate  
•  Sex at conception is biologically random and determined before parents can condition inputs on it, providing exogenous variation.  
•  Hindu eldest-son norms imply that “having no son yet” strongly predicts continuing fertility as well as differential allocation across existing children.  This satisfies instrument relevance.  
•  The design allows us to decompose two causal channels:
  – Fertility-stopping (additional siblings that dilute resources)  
  – Within-family allocation (being the coveted eldest son vs. the “excess” sibling)  
•  We can implement the same design in 25 sub-Saharan African (SSA) DHS samples that lack strong eldest-son norms, letting us difference out general effects of family size or birth order from India-specific eldest-son favoritism.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable(s)
T1:  Completed family size (or, in mother-fixed-effects models, the number of younger siblings the child eventually has).  
T2:  “Ex-post favored child” dummy =1 if the child is the first son in the sibship; 0 otherwise.

Instruments
Z1:  First-two-birth sex mix =1 if the first two births are both girls (GG); 0 if at least one is a boy (BG, GB or BB).  
Z2 (robustness):  First birth is a girl (G vs. B).

Control (counterfactual)
•  Children born to mothers whose first two births include a boy (instrument =0).  
•  Cross-country control: children in SSA samples, where Z1 affects fertility much less.

Treatment “timing”
The instrument is realised at the second birth; treatment (additional births or altered allocation) unfolds afterwards.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1.  Random sex at birth  
 ‑ Plausibility: Biological fact, plus ultrasound-based sex-selection was still rare for first-parity births in 2005/06 (especially among Muslims & in low-tech states).  Will test balance and replicate in pre-ultrasound cohorts (1992/93 NFHS).

A2.  Relevance  
 ‑ Parents without a son continue child-bearing (well-documented in Indian data).  First-stage F-stats in past work >100; will verify.

A3.  Exclusion (Z affects outcomes only through T)  
 ‑ No direct biological channel from “GG” to height.  The concern is parental son-preference might also shift investment in earlier girls before the third birth.  We mitigate via:
   •  Child-sex*birth-order fixed effects that soak up pure gender bias.  
   •  Comparing to SSA where such a direct channel is negligible.

A4.  Monotonicity  
 ‑ Parents who would stop when they already have a son will never have more children when they have a son (credible given norms).

A5.  Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-family spillovers)  
 ‑ Reasonable at household level.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T1.  Sex-selective abortion / differential survival could make sex composition non-random.  
  • Restriction to 2nd-parity births that preceded diffusion of ultrasound (≤1998).  
  • Balance tests on baseline covariates by Z within India; placebo in SSA.  
  • Trim states & religions with skewed sex ratios at birth.

T2.  Heterogeneous treatment effects violate exclusion (e.g., parents may invest less in daughters if no son yet, before additional birth occurs).  
  • Include mother-fixed effects and child-age-in-months FE, so identification comes from within-family, across birth-order contrasts.  
  • Add controls for child age and survey month to capture timing.

T3.  Non-comparability of India and SSA samples.  
  • Triple-difference specification: instrument*India dummy identifies India-specific effect.  
  • Match by wealth quintile and maternal education; re-weight SSA to Indian covariate distribution (entropy balancing).

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R CODE OUTLINE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0.  Packages
# -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # fast high-dim FE and IV
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Data loading
# -------------------------------------------------
# Assume dfs merged India & SSA, one row per child
df <- fread("NFHS_DHS_childlevel.csv")

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Variable construction
# -------------------------------------------------
df[, india        := as.integer(country=="India")]
df[, birth_order  := as.integer(birthorder)]           # 1,2,3…
df[, girl         := as.integer(sex=="Female")]
df[, height_z     := as.numeric(haz)]
df[, weight_z     := as.numeric(waz)]

# Instrument: first two births both girls (mother-level)
setorder(df, mother_id, birth_order)
df[, first2girls := 0L]
df[birth_order<=2, 
   first2girls := as.integer(all(sex=="Female")), 
   by = mother_id]
df[, first2girls := max(first2girls), by = mother_id]   # propagate to all sibs

# Treatment 1: completed sibship size (observed in data)
df[, sibship_size := max(birth_order), by = mother_id]

# Control variables
controls <- c("child_age_months", "maternal_age", "maternal_edu",
              "maternal_height", "wealth_quintile", "urban")

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Main IV regression: India sample
# -------------------------------------------------
# FE: mother_id
form1 <- as.formula(paste(
  "height_z ~ sibship_size | mother_id + child_age_months |",
  "sibship_size ~ first2girls"))
iv_india <- feols(form1, data = df[india==1], cluster = ~mother_id)
summary(iv_india)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Triple-diff IV: pooled India + SSA
# -------------------------------------------------
df[, Z := first2girls*india]   # interaction instrument
form2 <- as.formula(paste(
  "height_z ~ sibship_size*india | mother_id + country + child_age_months |",
  "sibship_size ~ Z"))
iv_triple <- feols(form2, data = df, cluster = ~country+mother_id)
summary(iv_triple)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Robustness: placebo on vaccination status
# -------------------------------------------------
form_placebo <- as.formula(
  "BCG_vaccinated ~ sibship_size | mother_id + child_age_months | sibship_size ~ first2girls")
placebo <- feols(form_placebo, data = df[india==1], cluster = ~mother_id)
summary(placebo)
```

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. EXPECTED RESULTS
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Prior:  
•  Relevance: “GG” increases completed family size by ≈ 0.5–0.8 child in India; <0.1 in SSA.  
•  Second-stage: Each additional sibling lowers height-for-age z-score by ~0.07–0.10 σ in India.  
•  Triple-diff: The India-specific penalty will add ~0.05 σ relative to SSA, consistent with 0.3–0.4 of the overall India/SSA height gap being attributable to eldest-son driven fertility/ allocation.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (IV DESIGN)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C1. Instrument is relevant (first-stage F>10):            1  
C2. Instrument exogenous (sex at birth random):           0.5  
C3. Exclusion restriction credible (no direct channel):  0.5  
C4. Monotonicity (no defiers):                            1  
C5. No interference / SUTVA:                              1  
Total = 4 / 5 ⇒ generally strong but with two assumptions needing careful testing.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
End of research plan
